questions.prompt: A line predicts dressing minutes of 6 and 9 for two wound-care visits that took 8 and 8 minutes. What is its mean squared error on these two visits?
questions.explanation: The errors are -2 and 1; their squares are 4 and 1, and their mean is 5 / 2 = 2.5.
misconceptions: Averages the absolute errors, which is the MAE, not the squared error
Averages the signed errors, so a miss above cancels a miss below
Sums the squared errors without dividing by the number of visits

questions.prompt: At the current line, the slope of the loss with respect to w is 30 and the learning rate is 0.01. The current w is 2. What is w after one gradient step?
questions.explanation: A step moves against the slope: 2 - 0.01 × 30 = 1.7.
misconceptions: Moves with the slope, which climbs the loss instead of descending it
Subtracts the slope without multiplying it by the learning rate
Thinks a small learning rate leaves w unchanged after one step

questions.prompt: A three-nearest-neighbour screen scores a new client. The four training clients are at distances 1.5 (did not fall), 2.0 (fell), 2.5 (fell) and 4.0 (did not fall). What does it predict?
options: No fall, because the single nearest client did not fall
No fall, because two of the four clients did not fall
It cannot say until a line is fitted to the four clients
A fall, because two of the three nearest clients fell
questions.explanation: The three nearest are at 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5; two of them fell, so the majority vote is a fall.
misconceptions: Uses one neighbour in place of three
Votes over every training client instead of the nearest three
Thinks a neighbour model needs a fitted line; it only needs distances

questions.prompt: A screen will predict, at a nurse's first visit, whether a wound heals within eight weeks. Which column is the label?
options: The wound's area in square millimetres at the first visit
Whether the wound healed within eight weeks
The client's age in years at the first visit
The nurse's estimate of healing time, in weeks
questions.explanation: The label is the outcome the screen predicts; the other columns are known at the visit and are candidate features.
misconceptions: Takes the most important measurement for the label; it is a feature
Takes a client attribute for the label; it is a feature
Takes a guess made at the visit for the outcome itself

questions.prompt: Changing a walk time from seconds to tenths of a second can change which training rows a nearest-neighbour model calls nearest.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Distances add up the differences in every feature, so a feature measured in larger numbers weighs more; unscaled, its unit changes the neighbours.
misconceptions: Thinks a distance ignores the units of each feature

questions.prompt: An analyst has training, validation and test rows for a wound-care screen and three candidate models. What are the validation rows for?
options: Fitting the three models, together with the training rows
Reporting how the chosen model will do next year
Choosing among the three models and their settings
Checking the code runs before the training rows are used
questions.explanation: Validation rows take no part in fitting, so they compare candidates fairly; the test rows are kept for one final, honest score.
misconceptions: Merges validation into training, so nothing is left to choose with
Gives validation the test set's job; a score used to choose is flattering
Treats validation as a code check rather than a measure

questions.prompt: As a tree's depth grows from 1 to 15, its training accuracy rises to 1.00 while its validation accuracy peaks at depth 4 and then falls. What is the diagnosis and the remedy?
options: Underfitting: allow deeper trees and more leaves
Overfitting beyond depth 4: limit the depth
A leak: remove the validation rows and refit
A good fit: report the depth-15 tree as it is
questions.explanation: Past depth 4 the tree learns noise in the training rows: the training score keeps rising while the validation score falls.
misconceptions: Reads the low early scores as the whole story and adds flexibility
Mistakes a widening train-validation gap for a leak
Reads the training curve as the result

questions.prompt: A learning curve for a two-feature model shows training and validation AUC meeting at 0.55 as the rows grow from 200 to 4,000. What will most likely help?
options: Collecting another 4,000 rows
A stronger penalty on large weights
Removing the validation rows from the curve
Better features or a more flexible model
questions.explanation: Both curves have met at a low score: the model underfits, so more rows add little and the model or its features must change.
misconceptions: Expects more rows to help a model that already learns all it can
Adds more simplicity to a model that is already too simple
Changes the measurement instead of the model

questions.prompt: Many wound-care clients have several visits. Why should the cross-validation folds be grouped by client?
options: So no client has visits in both a fold's fitting and scoring parts
So each fold has the same share of long visits as the whole data set
So the folds are smaller and run faster on a laptop
So the test set can be used as an extra, sixth fold
questions.explanation: Visits of one client resemble each other; if they sit on both sides, the model is scored on someone it has seen.
misconceptions: Describes stratified folds, which balance the label, not the clients
Thinks grouping is about speed
Mixes the test set into model choice

questions.prompt: In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression, a smaller C means a weaker penalty on large weights.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: C is the inverse of the penalty's strength: a smaller C means a stronger penalty and a simpler model.
misconceptions: Reads C as the penalty's strength rather than its inverse

questions.prompt: A screen predicts, at booking, whether a client will miss a clinic appointment. Which column is a target leak?
options: Days between booking and the appointment, counted at booking
Number of appointments the client missed in the past year
A reminder-call outcome logged after the appointment
Whether the client lives alone, recorded at registration
questions.explanation: A note logged after the appointment can record the miss itself; it is not known at booking.
misconceptions: Known at booking, so it is a fair feature
A past count, known at booking; a strong feature is not a leak by itself
Known at booking and unrelated to the outcome's timing

questions.prompt: An export holds 8% repeated rows of the same visit, and the analyst splits it at random. What is the fix?
options: Use a more flexible model so the copies matter less
Keep the copies and use ten folds in place of five
Drop the copies after the split, in the test rows only
Drop repeated visit identifiers before any split
questions.explanation: Copies on both sides let the model be scored on rows it was fitted on; removing them before the split removes the leak.
misconceptions: Expects a flexible model to suffer less, when it exploits copies most
More folds keep the copies on both sides
Leaves copies inside training and misses those already shared

questions.prompt: Four steps are fitted on all 300 rows before cross-validation. Which one is most likely to inflate the score a great deal?
options: Scaling eight numeric columns to mean 0 and spread 1
Keeping the 20 of 2,000 columns most correlated with the label
Filling blank values with the median of each column
One-hot encoding a column with four sector names
questions.explanation: Choosing columns by their link to the label, with every label in view, rewards chance matches; the other steps learn little or nothing from the label.
misconceptions: Scaling learns no label information; its leak is usually tiny
Medians learn no label information; still fit them on training rows
Encoding names learns no label information

questions.prompt: An export has a column visits_total: the number of visits each client had over the whole export, which runs to last month. A screen will score clients at their first visit. What kind of problem is this column?
options: A temporal leak: it counts visits after the prediction date
A duplicate leak: it repeats the same visit in several rows
A preprocessing leak: it was scaled using all the rows
No problem: the column has a value for every single client
questions.explanation: At a first visit, later visits have not happened; a total over the whole export uses the future.
misconceptions: Confuses a future count with repeated rows
Confuses a future count with a fitting step
Treats 'present in the export' as 'known on the day'

questions.prompt: When a scaler and a model are put in one pipeline and the pipeline is cross-validated, the scaler is refitted on the training part of each fold.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Cross-validating a pipeline refits every step in each fold, so no fold's scoring rows shape its preparation.
misconceptions: Thinks a pipeline fits its steps once, on all rows

questions.prompt: A screen for a rare outcome reports a test accuracy of 0.93. Why must a baseline be reported next to it?
options: Because a no-model baseline is always more accurate than a model
Because the test set is too small to report a score on its own
Because predicting "no" for everyone may score about the same
Because accuracy cannot be computed without a baseline to divide by
questions.explanation: When few people have the outcome, a no-model baseline can reach a high accuracy; only the comparison shows what the model adds.
misconceptions: Thinks baselines win by default
Confuses a comparison with the size of the test set
Thinks a baseline is part of computing accuracy

questions.prompt: A visit-length model has a validation MAE of 6.1 minutes. Predicting the training median for every visit gives 6.3. What is the fair summary?
options: The model is accurate: six minutes is a small error
The model is worse than the baseline
The baseline leaks, so its score should be ignored
The model barely beats a naive baseline
questions.explanation: An error means something only next to a baseline; 0.2 minutes better than a constant is little.
misconceptions: Judges an error without a baseline
Reads a lower MAE as worse
Thinks a constant prediction can leak

questions.prompt: A notebook fixes random_state=101 for every model. What does that guarantee?
options: That the chosen model is the best one the data allow
The same numbers on a rerun with the same data and versions
That another seed would give exactly the same scores
That the test score will hold for next year's clients too
questions.explanation: A seed fixes the random draws, so a rerun repeats them; it says nothing about how much the result depends on that draw.
misconceptions: Confuses repeatable with optimal
Thinks a seed removes randomness from the method
Confuses repeatable with generalising

questions.prompt: An analyst scores four models on the test set and reports the best of the four test scores. What is wrong?
options: Choosing on the test set makes its best score flatter
Nothing: the test set was not used to fit any of the four models
Four models are too many to compare on a single test set
The analyst should have reported the mean of the four test scores
questions.explanation: Choosing on the test set turns it into a validation set; the reported number is no longer an honest estimate.
misconceptions: Thinks only fitting can bias a score, not choosing
Blames the number of models, not the use of the test set
Averaging still mixes choice into the test score

questions.prompt: A language model is trained without any labels, so held-out testing does not apply to it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Its label is the next piece of text, and it is fitted by making a loss small; held-out tests, and leaks into them, matter as for any model.
misconceptions: Thinks text supplies no labels, and that scale exempts a model from testing

questions.prompt: Of 500 visits, 25 ran long. A screen flagged 40 visits, of which 10 ran long. What is its precision?
questions.explanation: Precision is caught over flagged: 10 / 40 = 0.25.
misconceptions: Computes recall: 10 of the 25 long visits
Computes accuracy: (10 + 445) / 500, dominated by the short visits
Computes the share flagged: 40 / 500

questions.prompt: A missed long visit costs 3 units and a needless extra slot costs 1. With calibrated scores, above which score should a visit be flagged?
questions.explanation: Flag when p × 3 exceeds (1 − p) × 1, that is when p is above 1 / (1 + 3) = 0.25.
misconceptions: Puts the missed cost on top: 3 / 4 is the share of cost in misses
Uses the library default, which ignores the costs
Divides the two costs, 1 / 3, which is a ratio and not the threshold

questions.prompt: A screen has precision 0.30 in a sector where 10% of clients fall. It is used unchanged in a sector where 30% fall and ranks clients equally well. What happens to its precision?
options: It stays at 0.30, because the model itself did not change at all
It rises, because more of the flagged clients are fallers
It falls, because the screen was fitted on a different sector
It cannot be compared across two sectors with different rates
questions.explanation: With the same ranking and more fallers, a larger share of the flagged clients fall, so precision rises with the base rate.
misconceptions: Thinks precision belongs to the model alone, not to the population
Confuses a base-rate change with a loss of ranking
Gives up on a comparison that the base rate explains

questions.prompt: A vendor's screen for an outcome that 5% of clients have reports 95% accuracy. What should you ask first?
options: Its recall: it may flag almost nobody
Its training accuracy, to compare
How many features it uses
Whether the 95% was rounded
questions.explanation: Flagging nobody gives 95% accuracy here; recall shows whether any client with the outcome is caught.
misconceptions: Training scores flatter and do not answer the question
The number of features says nothing about what it misses
Rounding is not the issue; the base rate is

questions.prompt: Lowering a screen's threshold can never lower its recall.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A lower threshold flags every client flagged before and possibly more, so caught cases cannot fall; precision may fall instead.
misconceptions: Confuses recall with precision, which can fall as the threshold drops

questions.prompt: A wound screen does not use age as an input but uses a column of years since the client registered. How do you test whether that column carries age?
options: Check that age does not appear anywhere in the list of the model's inputs
Compare the screen's overall AUC with and without the column
Ask the nurses whether they think the column is about age
Predict the age band from the column; compare with guessing the largest band
questions.explanation: If the column predicts the age band far better than guessing the largest band, it carries the attribute into the model.
misconceptions: Takes an absent input for an absent effect
Measures overall performance, not what the column encodes
Replaces a measurement with an opinion

questions.prompt: A screen flags 40% of visits in its first clinics and 95% in a newly opened one. Which first step is most likely to find the cause?
options: Refit the screen on the new clinic's visits straight away
Lower the threshold for the new clinic until the rate drops
Compare the clinic's input means with the training period
Wait for the outcomes, then compute the new clinic's AUC
questions.explanation: A jump in flags with no outcomes yet points to changed inputs, such as a new unit or protocol; input means by clinic show it at once.
misconceptions: Refits before knowing whether the data are wrong
Moves the threshold the wrong way and treats a symptom
Waits months, and a ranking score can hide a unit change

questions.prompt: A wound-infection screen's recall is 0.82 for clients who live with family (120 infections) and 0.61 for clients who live alone (70 infections). What belongs under 'who should not rely on it' in the model card?
options: Nobody: the overall recall is acceptable
Clients who live alone: a low score is weaker evidence, so nurses check the wound directly
Clients with family: they are flagged more often, so their flags are wrong
Everyone: any gap makes a screen unusable
questions.explanation: The measured gap means a low score for a client living alone rules out less; the card says so and says what staff do instead.
misconceptions: Hides a measured gap behind the overall number
Confuses being flagged more with being flagged wrongly
Turns a reported limit into a refusal to use the screen

questions.prompt: Who should review the model card that the analyst prepared for a home-care screen?
options: A different role, such as the quality and data protection officer
The analyst who built it, because the analyst knows the model best
Nobody needs to, as long as the notebook runs from end to end
The person on the team with the highest score in the capstone
questions.explanation: Separating the roles means the person who built the model does not review or approve it; the owner of the decision accepts it.
misconceptions: Lets the builder check their own work
Confuses a reproducible notebook with a reviewed one
Picks a reviewer by skill rather than by role

questions.prompt: If sex is not among a screen's inputs, the screen's recall cannot differ between women and men.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Inputs can be recorded differently by group, and other columns can carry the attribute, so error rates can still differ and must be measured.
misconceptions: Takes an absent input for an absent effect
